text: - That the Department of Health should ensure that training in the assessment of suicidal risk should be provided both to medical undergraduates and also to doctors working in Emergency Departments.      Local Health Networks have formal structures in place to provide training to medical undergraduates and Emergency Department clinicians in mental health assessment. This training includes a focus on suicide risk assessment.      The Office of the Chief Psychiatrist is also working with universities and professional organisations to enhance the training for assessments and responses to people with suicidal ideation in emergency and other health settings.      The South Australian Suicide Prevention Strategy 2012-2016 provides           a coordinated approach to service delivery, resources and information, and targeted suicide prevention and postvention initiatives, activities and programs. The Minister’s Suicide Prevention Advisory Committee, in collaboration with the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist, will oversee the Strategy, which will include regular monitoring of progress on actions outlined in the implementation guide. Annual Report of the State Coroner 2012-2013                                                       Page 28      SA Health has released Guidelines for Working with the Suicidal Person      (Attachment 1) to support and inform clinical assessment, decision-making and transfer of care in relation to people who may be feeling suicidal or experiencing suicidal ideation. These Guidelines have been modelled on similar guidelines produced by the Victorian and New South Wales governments.

- That a junior doctor or a mental health nurse should not discharge a suicidal patient, particularly one brought in by police under section 57(1)(c) of the Mental Health Act 2009, from an Emergency Department without having sought advice from a senior medical colleague - either an Emergency Department senior registrar or consultant, or else a psychiatric registrar or consultant on-call.      Local Health Networks have emphasised to all staff the protocol that the decision to discharge a patient with suicide risk from the Emergency Department should only be made in consultation with a senior medical officer.      Appropriate procedures are in place for Emergency Department staff to consult with either a psychiatric registrar or Consultant Psychiatrist 24 hours a day.

- That a minimum set of information should be obtained before discharging a suicidal patient from the Emergency Department. It would also be appropriate wherever possible to obtain information both from family members and from current treatment doctors or other therapists. This sometimes might not be possible until the next day when an individual presents to the Emergency Department overnight.      This recommendation has been implemented by the Local Health Networks. Processes are in place to ensure that clinical information for patients with mental health presentations is tracked via the existing electronic databases.      The Office of the Chief Psychiatrist developed the Mental Health Practitioner’s Guide to Sharing Consumer Information to operationalise the information sharing provisions of the Mental Health Act 2009. These were rolled out in 2011 and 2012 with education and training to metropolitan and country mental health services, emergency departments, other agencies such as SA Ambulance Services and the SA Police, and consumer and carer groups.

- There should be assertive follow-up of suicidal patients. They should be offered by community mental health services, with expectations about timely face to face follow-up.    Follow-up should be routinely offered to such patients and community mental health teams should be assertive and persistent in their attempts to see them face to face.      Client follow-up requirements are assessed and coordinated by the Mental Health Teams and are dependent on each case presentation. Local Health Networks have processes in place, or are currently reviewing their processes, to support the assertive follow-up on suicidal patients.      Other work being undertaken in relation to the assertive follow-up of people who are at risk of suicide includes:     The trial of 24-hour Assessment and Crisis Interventions Service (ACIS) Teams at metropolitan Local Health Networks, which began in later 2012.     The establishment at one Local Health Network of a new initiative that involves an integrated psychotherapy team following up patients with depression for four weeks in the crucial transition period from the Emergency Department to home. This team also has a Non-Government Organisations (NGO) psychosocial component that is Annual Report of the State Coroner 2012-2013                                                      Page 29 integrated as part of the service model. The protocol of this team is to see patients in Emergency Department and follow-up within 24 hours face to face.     A new series of eight polices, called the Pathways to Care Policies, are currently being developed and will replace the existing Emergency Demand Management policy suite. Discharge planning is an important component of the policy series and is referred to as transferring care. The term ‘discharge’ has been replaced by ‘transfer of care’ to emphasise the importance of continuity of care during transition from one service setting to another or to the community and General Practitioner.     The Office of the Chief Psychiatrist has undertaken extensive consultation with

- That domestic violence services and agencies throughout South Australia be encouraged to routinely divulge to SAPOL any information in the possession of the service or agency to the effect that the alleged perpetrator of domestic violence may have possession of or access to a firearm.      All women referred to Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services from the Domestic & Aboriginal Family Violence or Homelessness Gateway have a risk assessment completed which includes information relating to firearms.      All women presenting to Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services, through either the Gateway or direct, undergo an internal assessment which also includes a question pertaining to whether an alleged perpetrator of domestic violence may have possession of or access to a firearm.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will notify SAPOL, via the Notification Register Form, of any information that indicates an alleged perpetrator of domestic violence may have possession of or access to a firearm.      If a woman is identified as high risk, the woman’s information will also be provided to the Family Safety Framework Meeting.

- That domestic violence services and agencies throughout South Australia be encouraged to maintain individual records in relation to serial or repeat domestic violence perpetrators.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will develop their own perpetrator database that contains information in relation to serial or repeat domestic violence perpetrators.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services’ risk assessment forms will include a question pertaining to previous partners of a perpetrator of domestic violence.

- That domestic violence services and agencies throughout South Australia be encouraged to inform SAPOL of suspicions of breach of bail agreements and intervention orders by alleged perpetrators of domestic violence.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will report known breaches of bail agreements and intervention orders to SAPOL.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will report and document all known breaches of bail agreements and intervention orders in client case files, including the SAPOL response to the notification of the breach.      Currently Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services rely on their clients to provide them with information about intervention orders. The Department for Communities and Social Inclusion will continue negotiations towards the development of an Intervention Order notifications processes to notify funded Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services. - That domestic violence services and agencies throughout South Australia be encouraged to make repeated enquiry of alleged domestic violence victims as to whether or not the alleged perpetrator is complying with conditions of bail or with an intervention order.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will continue to ask domestic violence victims as to whether or not the alleged perpetrator is complying with conditions of bail or intervention orders in the risk and safety assessments and the formal case management response.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will embed the practice of making repeated enquiries of domestic victims as to whether or not the alleged perpetrator is complying with conditions of bail or with an intervention order by including the requirement in their practice policies.      Domestic/Aboriginal Family Violence services will document all enquiries made of domestic victims as to whether or not the alleged perpetrator is complying with conditions of bail or with an intervention order in client case notes. Registry Report The Manager of the Coroners Court has responsibility to oversee the financial and administrative functions of the office. The Manager also has a number of responsibilities delegated from the Coroner in order to manage a range of quasi- judicial functions as designated by the legislation. There are 14.7 full time equivalent (FTE) administrative staff (this number includes locum social workers) plus 2 FTE Counsel Assisting positions attached to the Coroners Court.
